# Walther Dobbertin

Walther Alexander Dobbertin was a German photographer, publisher, and author who documented colonial life in German East Africa during the early twentieth century . His extensive body of work provides one of the most comprehensive visual records of German colonial activities in East Africa, particularly during World War I, when he served as the sole combat photographer on the German side .

## Early Life and Background

Walther Alexander Dobbertin was born on August 28, 1882, in Berlin, Germany, to a working-class family . His ancestors originated from Mecklenburg, where the Kloster Dobbertin monastery is located . In Rostock, he completed a photography apprenticeship and attended painting courses .

## Career in German East Africa

In 1903, Dobbertin emigrated to German East Africa (Deutsch-Ostafrika), settling initially in Dar es Salaam . After working for several years in Carl Vincenti's photography studio in Dar es Salaam, a dispute arose between the two men in 1907 . Vincenti accused Dobbertin of stealing or embezzling photographic materials, resulting in Dobbertin's conviction and a three-day prison sentence .

Following this incident, Dobbertin established his own businesses. He founded book and art shops in Dar es Salaam, Tanga, and Moshi . During this period, he developed into one of the most prominent photographers in German East Africa . His photographs documented various aspects of colonial life, including political, social, economic, and military events . His subjects ranged from landscapes and wildlife to portraits of indigenous people and German settlers .

## World War I Documentation

The outbreak of World War I in 1914 presented a significant opportunity for Dobbertin's career as a photographer. When all German men were mobilized in August 1914 to defend the colony, he became, in effect, the only combat photographer on the German side . His documentation of military campaigns, daily life in the colony, and the activities of the German Schutztruppe (colonial defense force) provided an invaluable visual record of the conflict in East Africa .

In 1916, Dobbertin was captured by British forces while serving as a member of the German Schutztruppe . He remained in British captivity until the end of the war. Following the German defeat, all Germans were expelled from East Africa and their property was confiscated . However, Dobbertin's wife, Alwine, managed to smuggle his photographic plates out of the country .

## Return to Germany and Later Life

After his release from captivity, Dobbertin returned to Germany and settled in Wiedenhof, now part of Jesteburg, south of Hamburg . There, he established another bookshop .

In 1932, Dobbertin published a collection of glorifying portraits of German colonial soldiers titled "Die Soldaten Lettow-Vorbecks. Ein Buch vom deutschen Wehrwillen und deutscher Waffenehre" (Lettow-Vorbeck's Soldiers: A Book of German Fighting Spirit and Military Honor) . This work contained 120 photogravures of his photographs from German East Africa . An English-language edition was published in Nashville in 2005 .

During the Nazi era (1933-1945), Dobbertin was a member of the Sturmabteilung (SA) and served as Kreisleiter (district leader) of the Reichskolonialbund (Reich Colonial League) . After World War II ended in 1945, the British occupation authorities revoked his license to operate his business due to these activities . He later regained permission to operate his bookshop, which he ran until 1960 .

Dobbertin died on January 12, 1961, in Jesteburg-Wiedenhof, shortly before a planned trip to Africa, which would have been his first visit since his return in 1920 .

## Legacy and Collections

After Dobbertin's death, his widow sold his personal documents, photographic plates, and photographs to the Bundesarchiv (German Federal Archives), where they were preserved . In 2014, the Bundesarchiv published 982 of Dobbertin's photographs on Wikimedia Commons .

The German National Archives in Koblenz holds Dobbertin's original glass negatives (913 cm) and makes medium-resolution scans available to the public . The high quality of his work is evident in the large format of his negatives, which produce very sharp images with pronounced depth of field .

Dobbertin's photographs continue to be used in contemporary research and exhibitions. The Usambara Knowledge Project at Utah State University uses more than thirty of his early twentieth-century landscape photographs from the Usambara Mountains in northeastern Tanzania as a foundation for community-based history and oral history collection .

## Notable Publications

In addition to his 1932 book on Lettow-Vorbeck's soldiers, Dobbertin published or illustrated several other works:

1. "Hermann Löns, Grün ist die Heide. Eine Auswahl von 25 der besten Novellen, Jagd-, Tier- und Naturgeschichten. Mit 112 Lichtbildern aus dem gleichnamigen Film und Nachaufnahmen von Walther Dobbertin" (Hannover 1932)

2. "Alfred Funke, Schwarz-Weiß-Rot über Ostafrika. Roman. Mit 126 Lichtbildern von Walter Dobbertin" (Hannover 1933)

## Conclusion

Walther Dobbertin's work as a photographer provides an extensive visual record of German colonialism in East Africa during a crucial period of history. His documentation of military campaigns, daily life, and landscapes offers valuable insights into the colonial experience from a European perspective. While his Nazi-era activities must be acknowledged, his photographic legacy remains significant for historical research and contemporary understanding of German colonial history.

His photographs are preserved in the Bundesarchiv and continue to be studied by historians, anthropologists, and photographers. The high technical quality of his work, combined with its historical importance, ensures his place as a significant figure in the documentation of German colonialism in East Africa.

# Conditions Governing Use 

The Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa is the physical property of the 

Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University. Literary rights, including copyright, belong 

to the authors or their legal heirs and assigns. For further information, consult the appropriate curator. 

# Preferred Citation 

Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa. General Collection, Beinecke Rare 

Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University. 

# Processing Information 

Collections are processed to a variety of levels, depending on the work necessary to make them usable, 

their perceived research value, the availability of sta, competing priorities, and whether or not further 

accruals are expected. The library attempts to provide a basic level of preservation and access for all 

collections, and does more extensive processing of higher priority collections as time and resources 

permit. 

This collection received a basic level of processing, including rehousing and minimal organization. 

This finding aid may be updated periodically to account for new acquisitions to the collection or 

revisions in arrangement and description. 

Information included in the Content Description note and Collection Contents section is drawn 

from information supplied with the collection and from an initial survey of the contents. Portions 

of description for this collection have been directly repurposed from description supplied with the 

collection upon its receipt. Folder titles appearing in the contents list below are often based on those 

provided by the creator or previous custodian. Titles have not been verified against the contents of the 

folders in all cases. Otherwise, folder titles are supplied by sta during initial processing. 

Upon receipt, the collection was titled "From Cape to Cairo collection," as assigned by Humphrey 

Winterton and Maggs Brothers. The collection title was changed during processing in 2020. 

# Scope and Contents 

This collection consists of photograph albums, loose photographs, memorabilia and published material 

that document a European colonialist perspective of Africa and Egypt, and document both African peoples 

and European colonizers. Locations depicted in the photographs include Cameroon, Dar es Salaam, Egypt, 

Kenya, Namibia, Sudan, Tanga, Zambia, other regions throughout Africa, as well as some in Europe. 

Identified photographers in this collection include Alfredo Augusto Freire de Andrade, Walther Dobbertin, 

Paul Karl Lieberenz, and Carl von Vincenti. The bulk of photographs in the collection are created by 

unidentified photographers. 

# Arrangement 

Organized into seven series: I. Southern Africa, 1890 - 1929. II. Central Africa, circa 1918. III. East Africa, 1887 -

2005. IV. West Africa, 1880 - 1934. V. North Africa, 1904 - 1935. VI. Travel in Africa and Egypt, 1910 - 1920. VII. 

Colonial documentation of Africa, 1910 - 1933.

# Series I: Southern Africa, 1890–1929 

This series contains photograph albums and photographs documenting African colonial subjects, German 

colonialists, as well as wildlife in locations including Lourenco Marques, Transvaal, and Namibia. Also

This group of 50 mounted photographs contains images that document the 

delineation of the border between British and Portuguese territories in South 

East Africa, namely Portuguese-held Lourenco Marques and the Transvaal. 

Photographs include images of African colonial subjects, Lourenco Marques, the 

ocers of the Mozambique Expedition, the armoury, and the arrival of boats

This group of 60 photographic reproductions document German colonialists in 

Namibia. Included is a portrait of photographer G. Lange, along with inscriptions 

added to additional photographs by Lange. 

Founded in 1892 on the north coast of Namibia, Swakopmund quickly became 

the main harbour for the German colonialists in South West Africa. It received 

municipal status in 1909. The sketch map and many of the photographic images 

show the transport, principally rail, and route from the port of Swakopmund to 

the inland capital of Windhuk. The photographs depict warehouse life, train and 

railway stations in Kubas, Abbabis, Karibib, and Kaiser Wilhelmsberg. Images 

document scenes of the Schutztruppen arriving by ship, in parades, on patrol, and 

in combat scenes.

African colonial subjects, documenting several families and individuals, an image 

of two unidentified men at Omaruru in 1897 inscribed with, "After the funeral of 

Frau Odendaal," mounted elephants drinking in a river, and a herd of cattle.

b.  16  Tanga photograph album by Walther Dobbertin 

This album of 12 platinum photographs depicts the city of Tanga, including 

street scenes, the hospital, African huts, an old fortress, and the road to the 

cemetery. The cover of the album reads, "12 Bilder aus Deutsch-Ost-Afrika 

vom Kunstverlage Walther Dobbertin. Daressalam and Tanga D.O. Afrika, 

Serie IV. Tanga" 

circa 1905 

Unidentified photographers 

This series contains photograph albums and photographs by unidentified 

photographers. Locations depicted include Aden, Dar es Salaam, Egypt, Ethiopia, 

Kenya, Kilindini, Port Amelia, Rwanda, Saranda, Tanganyika, Uganda, Yemen, and 

Zanzibar. Subjects documented include street scenes, city views, architecture, 

German troops, African colonial troops, African colonial subjects, and colonial 

expeditions. 

Material is arranged alphabetically by subject. 

1887–1919 

b.  17  Aden and Zanzibar photographs 

This group of 14 photographs depicts Zanzibar and Aden from 1890 to 1910. 

Images include a view of Zanzibar harbour, a group photograph featuring 

Sayyid Hamad bin Thuwaini with four African advisors, Lloyd Mathews, the 

Prime Minister of Zanzibar, and Sir Arthur Harding. Other images include a 

street scene in Dar es Salaam, Sultan's palace, Boma of Bagamoyo, the clis 

at Aden harbour, and German soldiers, hunters, and ocers. 

1890-1910 

Walther Dobbertin (continued)

Container  Description  Date 

b.  18  Dar es Salaam, Kilindini, Port Amelia, and Saranda photograph album 

Kilindini became a significant harbour with the commencement of the 

construction of the Uganda Railway. HMS Challenger was moved to the East 

Africa Station in 1915 in order to take part in operations against the German 

ship SMS Königsberg in the Rufijii River. 

This album contains 160 photographs from August and September, 1916. The 

images depict several ports along the East African coast during World War 

I. The first part of the album documents Kilindini, the port at Mombasa, and 

includes images of the HMS Challenger and Vengeance, and damage to the 

docks. 

The album includes images of Mombasa itself, Dar es Salaam and Saranda 

in Tanganyika, and to the south a photo of Port Amelia in Mozambique. 

In addition there are views of African dhows, dwellings and farms, the 

Governor's residence and much of the infrastructure on the coast. 

1916 August -

September 

b.  19  East Africa, Egypt, Kenya, and Yemen photograph album 

This photograph album contains 163 images with individual, handwritten 

captions taken in Dar es Salaam, Aden, Lindi, Massassi, Nyangao, Zanzibar, 

Tanga, Mombasa, Suez and Port Said. The photographs depict naval craft, 

markets, village life, street scenes, and city views. Individuals documented 

include both German and colonial troops. The album also includes an image 

of a funeral for a German soldier, which bears Carl Vincenti's stamp in the 

bottom right hand corner. 

1905-1906 

b.  20  East Africa photograph albums 

2 Folders 

These two photograph albums contain 96 photographs of Dar es Salaam. 

The albums are bound, and titled, "Bilder aus Deutsch-Ostafrika." One album 

has a corresponding list of photograph captions. The first album depicts 

gatherings of African colonial subjects, including archery competitions, 

groups of women, dancing, and ceremonies. 

The second album appears to document an expedition primarily around 

Tanganyika. Images depict boats and canoes, porters transporting luggage 

and other supplies across rivers and over land to a series of villages 

in Tabora, Zanzibar as well as Dar es Salaam. The album also includes 

photographs of pottery production in Burundi and a tea plantation in 

Rwanda. 

1910 

b.  21  East Africa photograph album 

This album contains 144 photographs with individual handwritten captions 

on the eve of the World War I. Images depict Dar es Salaam including the 

sea trade, ocean liners and barges in the harbour, and African fisherman in 

small sailboats. This album also contains photographs that depict a series 

of houses in Dar es Salaam and the surrounding regions of Lindi, Morogoro, 

Sekenke, Singida, and Ngago, including a workhouse, the Governor's house, 

and European and African dwellings. Also included are images that appear to 

follow a train journey out into the countryside, including many photographs 

of African colonial subjects, agriculture, mission stations as well as the 

occasional images of the expedition itself. 

circa 1912 

Unidentified photographers (continued)

GEN MSS 1606 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  22  East Africa and Egypt photograph album 

This album contains 103 photographs, cigarette cards, and other ephemera. 

It appears the owner of the album served on the SMS Königsberg. Early in the 

album there is an image of a group of five ocers from the ship. Königsberg 

was the lead ship in the German Imperial Navy, and is best known for service 

during the First World War. 

The album includes three panoramas of Dar es Salaam, as well as depictions 

of the harbor, African dwellings, colonial bridges, and African porters 

transporting goods. The album also contains photographs of the Maasai 

people and African colonial subjects. The images include dancing, hair 

dressing, jewellery, clothing, children, bathing, grinding wheat, tribal 

councils, and a series of colonial encounters. The album closes with a few 

photographs of Egypt, a picture of Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck and Schnee in 

Berlin, ephemera relating to Cairo and East Africa and two images of soldiers 

in Nazi uniforms. Several photographs depict the racist practice of blackface. 

1914-1919 

b.  23  Italian Eritrea Expedition photograph album 

This album of the Italian Eritrea Expedition contains 115 photographs with 

handwritten captions and a large folding 1895 colour lithograph map of 

Eritrea in the rear pocket. 

This album documents the arrival of Italian colonialists in Northern Ethiopia 

at the beginning of the Italy-Abyssinia war, 1887-1889. The album also 

includes images of Dogali, where Ras Alula, the Ethiopian general, achieved 

victory over the Italians in January 1887. 

The album contains images that depict Suez, Port Said and the Canal, the 

pyramids and the Sphinx. There are thirty photos of Massawa and its port. 

Other images include vaccinations being administered to African patients, 

group portraits of the medical corps, ocers, African commanders, military 

installations, Assab, Otumlo, the Swedish Mission at Moncullo, Dogali and 

the camp of Ras Alula, Fort Borelli, Fort Victor Emanuele, and Massawa 

Saati. The album concludes with images of of families, soldiers, housing, and 

villages. 

1887–1895 

b.  13  Kenya, Uganda, and Tanganyika photograph album 

This album of Kenya, Uganda, and Tanganyika during World War I contains 

123 photographs with handwritten captions. Although the East Africa 

Campaign had eectively finished by November 1917, the German army 

remained active a year later. Taken in mid-1918, the images contained 

in this album depict the medical facilities in East Africa at the time. The 

photographs include hospital sta and British and Kenyan soldiers, many 

of whom are identified by name. The Carrier Hospital at Lindi (Tanganyika) 

and the Sanitorium at Kijabe (Kenya) are well documented. The album 

also includeds images of Dar es Salaam and Lindi, waterbuck and eland at 

Bukoba, Chania Falls at Thika, the remains of a German wireless at Mwanza, 

a German fort at Mwanza, Bukoba, Entebbe, CMS Hospital at Kampala, the 

Nile at Jinja and Victoria Nyanza, SS Ebani, and the fort at Mombasa, B.E.A. 

1918 

b.  24  Panoramic photograph of Rwanda by unidentified photographer (Vater) 

This four print panorama looks toward the three volcanoes in the Virunga 

Mountains from what appears to be a tea plantation. At a conference 

in Brussels in 1890, Germany was granted both Rwanda and Burundi in 

exchange for relinquishing all claims to Uganda. The photograph is inscribed 

with the name "Vater." 

1909 April 19

# Series IV: West Africa, 1880–1934 

This series contains photograph albums and photographs depicting locations including Cameroon, Lomé, 

Portugal, Senegal, and Togo. Images document German plantations, trains, African peoples, landscapes, 

German colonialists, and architecture. 

Material is arranged alphabetically by subject. 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  25  Cameroon photograph album by Paul Karl Lieberenz 

This album, titled "Nord-Kamerun" of Cameroon contain 66 photographs taken by 

the German colonial photographer Paul Karl Lieberenz. The album includes four 

panoramic photographs, a colour illustration marking the German plantations in 

Cameroon, mainly palm oil, cocoa, banana, and gum, as well as a small sketch map. 

Photographs in the albums document Lieberenz's travels in North Cameroon in 

1933-34. Images include colonial depictions of the life and customs of Indigenous 

tribes native to Cameroon, including those living in Pirate Islands, and towns and 

villages of Buea, Mbemi, Bali, Babanki Tungo, Babungo, Banso, and Kumbo. 

Other locations and scenes depicted in the photographs include Mount 

Cameroon, the seaside city of Victoria (Limbe), Bota Island, Fernando Po (Bioko, 

Bioco), Bamenda (Abakwa and Mankon Town), the volcanic landscape of Babanki 

Tungoh, the historic fortress of Bamenda, the residence of von Puttkamer in Buea, 

a Mamfe tomb, banana plantations in Tiko, a Banso-warrior, ceremonial dance, a 

crowded local market, Mbemi women preparing palm oil, an African man climbing 

up a coco tree, skilled woodcarvers of Babanki Tungo, African people crossing the 

Mungo River, and glimpses of steelmakers extracting iron in the charcoal ovens. 

1933-1934 

b.  26–27  Cameroon and Togo photographs 

10 Folders 

This group of 98 photographs of Cameroon and Togo includes mounted 

photographs, a three-print panorama, and postcards. Many have German captions 

in pencil on the verso. The images depict trains and passengers at a station, 

scenes at sea, including one of Monrovia, rural scenes with people, and colonialists 

and African people. Of the 43 larger images, seven are identified on the verso as 

being of Togo and 29 as Cameroon, with the remaining seven unidentified. The 

panorama shows the mission in Nyasono in south-west Cameroon. 

Other images depict landscapes, animals, and infrastructure such as bridges and 

railways, ships and boats on the Atlantic, waterways, rivers, and harbors. Also 

included is a glass plate negative box that was used to house photographs. 

1897-1905 

b.  27  Lomé, Togo panoramic photograph 

This folding nine-image panorama of Lomé, Togo stretches from the coast to 

the medical center. Thirty-four buildings are numbered including the post oce, 

the government school, factories, military barracks, and the train station. The 

panorama is housed in a bound book, and titled, "Panorama von Lome, Hauptitadt 

des Togogebietes" 

1905 

Page  13  of  20 Series IV: West Africa  Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa 

GEN MSS 1606 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  28  Luanda, Cabinda, Sao Thome, Costa d'Ouro and Sao Miguel photograph album 

This album contains 92 photographs. The album pages have been removed from 

the album binding. Images depict colonial buildings in Cabinda and Luanda, such 

as the governor's residence, military barracks, the hospital, a pharmacy, bridges, 

a cocoa factory, the Roca de Santa Virginia Mission, and views of Costa d'Ouro, 

Funchal, Madeira, Sao Miguel, and Sao Thome. 

Photographs also depict group images of African people from Sao Thome, Cabinda 

and Malarige, as well as people harvesting sugar cane, musicians, and an inland 

expeditionary group. 

circa 1880s 

b.  27  Senegal photographs 

This group of 14 photographs depicts the Bassari people, goods being transported 

across the Hamansu River, Ho Station, Bimbila Station, Misahohe Station, farming 

in Uapuli, a view over Bassari, the construction of a hut, a group of Islamic school 

students, views of Kamanji and Atakpame, and the chief of Apai and his followers. 

undated 

b.  29  Togo photograph album 

This album of Togo contains 57 photographs documenting the German colonial 

period from 1910-1912. Also included is a postcard of Lomé and an original color 

map, marking the German protectorate. 

The album includes photographs of Togo, featuring towns and villages of Lomé, 

Sokodé, Banjeli, Palimé (Kpalimé), Misahöhe, and Sebe. The images reflect the 

life and environment of African people in Togo during the colonial period and 

show views from the port of Lomé, train tracks, and a German colonial station 

in Missahohé. Individuals and subjects depicted include an African woman with 

scarification, women miners of Banjeli, iron-smelting ovens, market scenes, views 

of Mount Agou (Mount Baumann) from the village, dam construction, colonial 

ocials and their families, German Colonial Police, and African interpreters in 

European suits. 

1910-1912 

Page  14  of  20 Series V: North Africa  Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa 

GEN MSS 1606 

# Series V: North Africa, 1904–1935 

This series contains photograph albums documenting locations including Egypt, France, Italy, and Sudan. 

Images document African peoples, military troops, street scenes, and big game hunting. 

Material is arranged chronologically. 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  30  Egypt and Sudan photograph albums by Henry Maitland Wilson 

Field Marshall Lord Henry Maitland Wilson, G.C.B., G.B.E., D.S.O. (1881-1964) 

attended Eton and Sandhurst before being commissioned into the Rifle Brigade 

as a 2nd Lieutenant in May 1900. Nicknamed "Jumbo", Wilson's military career 

included service in the Boer War and World War I, before attaining the rank of 

General and overseeing operations in the Middle East and Mediterranean. 

Between 1939 and 1944, he held various commands in North Africa and the Middle 

East when he succeeded General Eisenhower as Supreme Allied Commander of 

the Mediterranean Theatre. He was a confidant of Winston Churchil and was 

made Field Marshall in 1944. Three years later he became Chief of the British Joint 

Sta Mission in Washington D.C. where his friendship with Eisenhower prospered 

(to the extent that Eisenhower provided an introduction to Wilson's volume of 

wartime memoirs). In 1944 he became Baron Wilson of Libya and of Stowlangtoft. 

These photograph albums document a hunting trip in Sudan and Egypt and 

contain 163 photographs with captions. One album is signed "HM Wilson Rifle 

Brigade" on the front pastedown. 

These albums record a hunting trip made with Field Marshall Lord Henry Maitland 

Wilson and fellow soldiers along the White Nile. Included are photographs of 

African communities, including the Shilluk people, the Baggara, the Nuer people, 

and the Dinka people. Other images depict big game hunting, fellow travellers, as 

well as markets, the boats on which they sailed, and life along the shores of the 

Nile. 

1904-1905 

b.  31  Egypt photograph album by G.A. Chadburn 

3 Folders 

This album of Egypt contains 78 photographs, 65 silk regimental arms, newspaper 

clippings, and two cotton maps of the Dardanelles, and of central Europe. 

Egypt allied itself with the Central Powers at the outbreak of war and these 

images present a rare insight to this arena. British troops struck early in order to 

secure the Anglo-Persian pipeline and withstood a counter attack in February 

1915. The album appears to belong to G.A. Chadburn from Stockport, whose card 

is taped to the front pastedown. There is also an image of soldiers from Cheadle 

Hulme, which is part of Stockport. 

The album includes images of troops in Cairo, Alexandria, Hadra Prison, Sakhara 

and Ismailia in the early months of the war. There is a selection of images 

featuring artillery, inspection lines, the Australian camp at Giza, US ships at 

Alexandria, and bridge building. 

Other images depict individuals traveling throughout Egypt, a picnic on the Nile 

on Easter Sunday, 1915, Egyptian fruit sellers, fishermen, and coast guards. The 

final photographs are of a military hospital in Reading. The newspaper clippings all 

relate to the Dardanelles campaign, particularly Gallipoli. 

circa 1910s 

Page  15  of  20 Series V: North Africa  Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa 

GEN MSS 1606 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  32  Egypt World War I photograph album 

This album contains 400 photographs documenting British troops in Egypt during 

World War I. The photographer was based in the British camp at Beni Salama, 

which is situated about 60 kilometers north west of Cairo on the western edge 

of the Nile delta. Photographs depict Egyptian people, firing practice, camp 

accommodations in the desert (tents, latrines), troops riding horseback and 

camels, meals, feluccas on the Nile, the sphinx and pyramids at Giza, street scenes 

in Cairo, the Muhammad Ali Mosque, and the ancient monuments at Luxor. The 

group portraits are of the Ocers of the Woolwich Sub-Command London AA 

Defences. 

1916 

b.  33  Egypt, France, Italy, and Sudan photograph album 

This album of Egypt, Sudan, Italy, Sicily and France contains 202 photographs. 

The annotations are detailed and provide information on the various ports and 

cities encountered. The bulk of this annotated album comprises photographs 

taken in Egypt and in Sudan as the photographer appears to have travelled down 

the Nile on the ship Straithaird. African communities represented include the 

Dinka people, the Shilluk people, the Nuer people, and the Bari people. Towns or 

ports documented include Taormina, Port Said, Port Sudan, Melut, Malakal, Sambe, 

Malek and Khartoum, before the photographer ventures back to northern Italy 

and the south of France, ending finally in Provence. 

1933–1935 

Page  16  of  20 Series VI: Travel in Africa and Egypt  Collection of photographs relating to European colonization in Africa 

GEN MSS 1606 

# Series VI: Travel in Africa and Egypt, 1910–1920 

This series contains photograph albums and photographs documenting locations including Algeria, Egypt, 

Ghana, Kenya, and other locations in Africa. Images depict big game hunting, European colonialists, African 

colonial subjects, and architecture. 

Material is arranged alphabetically by subject. 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  34–35  Africa and Egypt photograph albums 

These albums document a trip from Southern Africa to Cairo and contains 576 

photographs. The opening images in the first album are of Zambezi River at 

Victoria Falls. Images in the albums depict a big game hunting safari undertaken 

on both sides of the river in both Northern and Southern Rhodesia (present day 

Zambia and Zimbabwe). Images include the hunting party which consisted of 

the European colonialists and African people, as well as the game that was killed, 

including elephant, bualo, a lion and lioness, zebra, warthog, wild boar, hyena, gnu 

and antelope. Included is a series of photographs of young rhinos on a farm being 

hand-reared and bottle-fed, as well as young bualo being loaded into a crate and 

the onto a rear of a truck. 

Photographs in the second album depicts African people and European 

colonialists on big game hunts. Other images document an Ocean voyage, and 

scenes depicting the Sphinx and the Great Pyramid of Giza. The end of the album 

depictcts large European-style houses, ostriches and pelicans in cages. The 

remainder of the album include more images of Cairo and Giza, as well as images 

of individuals. 

circa 1920 

b.  31  Algeria, Ghana, and Kenya photographs 

This group of five photographs includes one of Algeria, inscribed, "Alger: La 

Kasbah: Rue de la Mer Rouge." Two other photographs are inscribed with "Accra" 

on the verso and depict the docks of Ghana. Two other photographs depict groups 

of Bantu peoples of Western Kenya. 

circa 1910

# Series VII: Colonial documentation of Africa, 1910–1933 

This series contains primarily printed material created by European colonialists about Africa. Included 

are volumes of photographic reproductions, published material, and a photograph album. The material 

documents how a colonial perspective of Africa was produced and distributed to a European audience. 

Material is arranged chronologically. 

Container  Description  Date 

b.  36–37  Die Deutschen Kolonien 

Two volume sets of bound photographic reproductions, with additional mounted 

photographic reproductions. The first set is divided into the following volumes: 

I. Togo, II. Kamerun, III. Deutsch-Südwestafrika. The second set contains the 

following volumes: I. Deutsch-Ost-Afrika, II. Kaiser-Wilhelmsland und die Inselwelt 

im Stillen Ozean, III. Samoa, IV. Kiautschou. 

All the photographic reproductions and plates are the work of three 

photographers: Dr Robert Lohmeyer, Bruno Marquardt and Eduard Kiewning. 

Printing was done by the Institute for Colour Photography, Carl Weller, Berlin. 

circa 1910 

b.  31  Deutschlands Kolonien by Willy Scheele 

First edition by Weller and Hüttich, Berlin. 1912. 63 of the 80 images and 124 pages 

of the text are devoted to the German colonies in Africa including Togo, Kamerun, 

Deutsch-Südwestafrika, and Deutsch-Ostafrika. 

1912 

b.  31  Farbfotografien aus den Deutschen Kolonien by Willy Scheel 

2 Folders 

48 color oset lithography reproductions with printed captions. Foreword by 

Dr. Scheel, including the narrative, "Overview of the German Colonies." The 48 

illustrations have been selected from the 80 which are included in Dr. Scheel's 

book. Though primarily devoted to German colonies in Africa, this set of images 

provides photographs of Togo, Cameroon, German Southwest Africa, German 

East Africa, New Guinea, Caroline Islands, the Bismarck Archipelago, Samoa, and 

Kiatschou Bay. 

All of the photographic reproductions and plates are the work of three 

photographers: Dr Robert Lohmeyer, Bruno Marquardt and Eduard Kiewning. 

Publication is by Carl Weller of the Institute for Colour Photography, Berlin. 

1913 

b.  38  Das Kolonial Wirtschaftliche Komitee Berlin Kolonial Ausstellung By Paul 

Lieberenz 

The Colonial Economic Development Committee of Berlin was founded in the late 

nineteenth century for the purpose of finding and identifying tropical plants and 

agricultural crops which could be commercially exploited. It mounted numerous 

expeditions for this purpose, frequently to remote areas not previously visited 

by Europeans. Its work was greatly hampered after Germany's loss of its colonies 

during and after the First World War. In the 1920s Germany was in political 

and economic turmoil and, by the end of 1930, parliamentary democracy had 

eectively given way to an increasingly authoritarian regime with the National 

Socialists gaining ground. Against this background, the politicians were looking 

for ways to restore Germany's influence abroad, including the former colonies. 

Original commemorative photographic album produced by Paul Lieberenz for 

the German Colonial Exhibition held in Berlin in May 1933. The album contains 

14 photographs, including a printed introductory essay by the Committee's 

Chairman, Dr. h. c. A. Drehn. 

There is documentation of the racist practice of including live humans in 

anthropological displays, featuring people from Africa who were brought over to 

Berlin to be used in the exhibition. 

1933

### Synopsis

**Deutsch:**[Walther Dobbertin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/de:Walther_Dobbertin "w:de:Walther Dobbertin") war ein deutscher Fotograf. Dobbertin wanderte 1903 nach Deutsch-Ostafrika aus, wärend des ersten Weltkrieges war er der einzige deutsche Fotograf der die Geschehnisse auf deutscher Seite dokumentierte. Nach der Kriegsgefangenschaft kehrte er nach Deutschland zurück, seine Arbeiten wurden von seiner Frau vor der Enteignung gerettet. 1932 veröffentlichte er eine Sammlung verherrlichender Soldatenportraits aus der deutsch-ostafrikanischen Kolonialzeit.

**English:** Walther Dobbertin was a German photographer who is most famous for his photographs of German East Africa where he emigrated in 1903. Dobbertin is the only German photographer who covered the East African Campaign of World War I. After leaving captivity as a prisoner of war Dobbertin settled in Germany. Most of his works were rescued from expropriation by his wife. In 1932 Dobbertin publishes a collection of glorifying portraits of german colonial soldiers.

2.title: Walther Dobbertin
2.content:
aus Wikipedia, der freien Enzyklopädie

**Walther Alexander Dobbertin** (* [28. August](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/28._August "28. August")[1882](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/1882 "1882") in [Berlin](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin")[[1]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-1); † [12. Januar](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/12._Januar "12. Januar")[1961](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/1961 "1961") in [Jesteburg-Wiedenhof](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesteburg "Jesteburg")[[2]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:1-2)) war ein deutscher Fotograf und Verleger, der hauptsächlich in der ehemaligen Kolonie [Deutsch-Ostafrika](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsch-Ostafrika "Deutsch-Ostafrika"), im Gebiet des heutigen [Tansania](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tansania "Tansania"), tätig war. Sein fotografisches Werk, das aus Hunderten von Schwarz-Weiß-Aufnahmen besteht, bietet eine umfassende Darstellung der politischen, sozialen, wirtschaftlichen und militärischen Aspekte der Kolonie. Seine Motive reichen von Landschaften und Wildtieren bis hin zu Porträts von Einheimischen und deutschen Siedlern. Vor allem dokumentierte er die Aktivitäten der deutschen [Schutztruppe](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schutztruppe "Schutztruppe") und in den Anfangsjahren des [Ersten Weltkriegs in Ostafrika](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erster_Weltkrieg_in_Ostafrika "Erster Weltkrieg in Ostafrika").

Dobbertin wurde als Kind einer Berliner Handwerkerfamilie geboren. Seine Vorfahren stammten aus [Mecklenburg](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mecklenburg "Mecklenburg"), wo sich das [Kloster Dobbertin](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloster_Dobbertin "Kloster Dobbertin") befindet. In [Rostock](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rostock "Rostock") durchlief er eine Fotografenlehre und besuchte Malkurse.[[3]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:0-3)

1903 wanderte Walther Dobbertin nach Deutsch-Ostafrika (DOA) aus. Nach seiner Ankunft arbeitete er für einige Jahre im [Fotostudio](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fotostudio "Fotostudio") von [Carl Vincenti](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Vincenti "Carl Vincenti") in Daressalam.[[4]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-4) 1907 kam es zwischen Vincenti und Dobbertin zu einem heftigen Streit, der vor Gericht ausgetragen wurde. Vincenti warf Dobbertin vor, fotografisches Material gestohlen bzw. unterschlagen zu haben.[[5]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:3-5) Dobbertin wurde daraufhin zu einer Gefängnisstrafe von drei Tagen und Übernahme der Gerichtskosten verurteilt.[[6]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-6)

Nachdem Dobbertin sich anschließend selbstständig gemacht hatte, gründete er in Daressalam, [Tanga](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanga_(Tansania) "Tanga (Tansania)") und [Moshi](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moshi_(Stadt) "Moshi (Stadt)") Buch- und Kunsthandlungen. Er entwickelte sich in den folgenden Jahren zu einem der bedeutendsten Fotografen Deutsch-Ostafrikas. Nach dem Ausbruch des [Ersten Weltkrieges](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erster_Weltkrieg "Erster Weltkrieg") war er der einzige Fotograf, der die Geschehnisse in der umkämpften Kolonie auf deutscher Seite dokumentierte.[[7]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-7)

1916 geriet Dobbertin als Mitglied der deutschen [Schutztruppe](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schutztruppe_f%C3%BCr_Deutsch-Ostafrika "Schutztruppe für Deutsch-Ostafrika") in englische Gefangenschaft. Bei Kriegsende wurden die Deutschen aus Ostafrika ausgewiesen und enteignet. Der Frau Dobbertins, Alwine, gelang es aber, die fotografischen Platten ihres Mannes außer Landes zu schmuggeln. Nach seiner Entlassung aus der Gefangenschaft kehrte Dobbertin nach Deutschland zurück und zog nach Wiedenhof, heute ein Ortsteil von [Jesteburg](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesteburg "Jesteburg"), südlich von [Hamburg](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg"). Dort eröffnete er erneut eine Buchhandlung.[[3]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:0-3)

1932 veröffentlichte Dobbertin unter dem Titel _Die Soldaten [Lettow-Vorbecks](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul\_von\_Lettow-Vorbeck "Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck")_. _Ein Buch vom deutschen Wehrwillen und deutscher Waffenehre_ im Selbstverlag eine Sammlung verherrlichender Soldatenporträts aus der deutsch-ostafrikanischen Kolonialzeit. Neben 120 [Kupfertiefdrucken](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiefdruckverfahren "Tiefdruckverfahren") seiner Aufnahmen in DOA enthält die englische Übersetzung von 2005 ein Nachwort über Dobbertins Leben.[[8]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-8) In der [Zeit des Nationalsozialismus](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeit_des_Nationalsozialismus "Zeit des Nationalsozialismus") war Dobbertin Mitglied der [SA](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sturmabteilung "Sturmabteilung") und [Kreisleiter](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kreisleiter "Kreisleiter") des [Reichskolonialbundes](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reichskolonialbund "Reichskolonialbund"). Wegen dieser Tätigkeiten wurde ihm 1945 von der britischen Besatzungsbehörde die Lizenz zum Betrieb seines Geschäftes entzogen. Nachdem er die Erlaubnis zurückerhalten hatte, betrieb er die Buchhandlung bis 1960. Kurz vor einer geplanten Reise nach Afrika, der ersten nach seiner Rückkehr im Jahre 1920, starb Dobbertin am 12. Januar 1961.[[3]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:0-3)[[2]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:1-2)

Nach seinem Tod verkaufte Dobbertins Witwe seine persönlichen Dokumente, Fotoplatten und Fotos an das [Bundesarchiv](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bundesarchiv_(Deutschland) "Bundesarchiv (Deutschland)"), wo sie archiviert wurden.[[9]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-9)

[![Image 1: People working on a railroad](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Bundesarchiv_Bild_105-DOA0958%2C_Deutsch-Ostafrika%2C_Sisalernte.jpg/250px-Bundesarchiv_Bild_105-DOA0958%2C_Deutsch-Ostafrika%2C_Sisalernte.jpg)](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Datei:Bundesarchiv_Bild_105-DOA0958,_Deutsch-Ostafrika,_Sisalernte.jpg)

Sisalernte in DOA

Dobbertins Fotografien des kolonialen Lebens in Deutsch-Ostafrika umfassen Hunderte von Bildern politischer, sozialer, wirtschaftlicher und militärischer Ereignisse, darunter Aufnahmen von Großwildjagd und Wildtieren, Naturlandschaften und dem Bau von Eisenbahnen. Seine Fotografien von Afrikanern zeigen die einheimische Bevölkerung und ihr Alltagsleben unter der Kolonialherrschaft. Dazu gehören Bilder von Askari-Soldaten der deutschen Schutztruppe ebenso wie anderer Bewohner der Kolonie, wie beispielsweise Inder und [Swahilis](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili_(Gesellschaft) "Swahili (Gesellschaft)"). Andere Bilder zeigen das Leben auf dem Land, darunter Afrikaner, die auf einer [Sisal](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisalfaser "Sisalfaser")plantage arbeiten oder Kinder am Ufer eines Flusses, die Einbäume zu Wasser lassen und fischen.[[10]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-10)

Neben schriftlichen Quellen und künstlerischen Abbildungen aus der Zeit vor der Verbreitung der Fotografie im 19. Jahrhundert dienen Fotografien aus dem kolonialen Afrika als Dokumente für die Erforschung der Geschichte des Landes und seiner Bewohner. In der akademischen Wissenschaft beschäftigen sich Disziplinen wie [visuelle Anthropologie](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visuelle_Anthropologie "Visuelle Anthropologie"), [Kulturwissenschaft](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kulturwissenschaft "Kulturwissenschaft") sowie die Geschichte der Fotografie mit solchen Fotografien. Die Kulturanthropologin Christraud M. Geary hat darauf hingewiesen, dass ihre Bedeutungen vielfältig sind und auf offene Weise interpretiert werden können. Als historische Dokumente zeugen sie von Kolonialherrschaft und den Lebensbedingungen der einheimischen Bevölkerung.[[11]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:2-11)

Ab Ende des 19. Jahrhunderts wurden Fotografien und Bildpostkarten bei Besuchern und Bewohnern europäischer Kolonien in Afrika und anderswo immer beliebter. Durch technische Verbesserung und relativ billige Postdienste schufen vor allem Postkarten, aber auch Abbildungen in Büchern und Zeitschriften neue Kommunikationsformen und dienten dabei vor allem kommerziellen und politischen Interessen. Damals wie heute haben diese Bilder das Bild wichtiger historischer Veränderungen im Leben der Afrikaner geprägt.[[11]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:2-11)

Im Vergleich zu dokumentarischen Fotografien, die von Kolonialoffizieren und Wissenschaftlern aufgenommen wurden, wurden weniger authentische Bilder von Afrika und seinen Völkern oft von kommerziellen Fotografen erstellt, die am schnell wachsenden Markt für Fotos und Postkarten aus Afrika beteiligt waren. Kommerzielle Fotostudios wie Dobbertins produzierten ansprechende und verkaufsfördernde Fotos, indem sie die Porträtierten in bestimmten Posen und oft mit „typischer“ Kleidung und Schmuck sorgfältig inszenierten. Ihre manipulierten Porträts trugen so zur [Stereotypisierung](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereotyp "Stereotyp") von Afrika und der Afrikaner bei.[[12]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-12) Im Rahmen [postkolonialer Studien](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postkolonialismus "Postkolonialismus") werden solche Darstellungen mit dem Begriff „[Kolonialer Blick](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kolonialer_Blick "Kolonialer Blick")“ bezeichnet.[[13]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-13)

Junge Afrikanerin

So diskutierte die Kunsthistorikerin für afrikanische Kunst Prita Meier in ihrer Studie, wie Frauen auf historischen Fotografien der Swahiliküste dargestellt wurde, Dobbertins Bild von 1906 von einer „einheimischen Frau mit Schmuck, Siedler und Junge“ als inszeniertes Beispiel für „die Privilegien, die weiße Männer in Afrika genießen.“[[14]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-14) Andere „exotische“ Fotografien von Dobbertin, die teilweise nackte afrikanische Frauen abbilden,[[15]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-15) sind Beispiele für die visuelle Darstellung von Afrikanerinnen durch Kolonialfotografen.[[11]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:2-11)

In Zeitschriften, Büchern und Studien über Deutsch-Ostafrika wurden Dobbertins Fotografien als historische Dokumente verwendet. So veröffentlichten deutsche Nachrichtenmedien wie [_Der_ _Spiegel_](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der_Spiegel "Der Spiegel")[[16]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-16) und die _[Deutsche Welle](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deutsche\_Welle "Deutsche Welle")_ Dobbertins Bilder, um militärische Ausbildung, Zwangsarbeit und andere Ereignisse zu dokumentieren, die durch deutsche und andere Kolonialmächte im Ersten Weltkrieg begangen wurden. Diese Bilder dienten als visuelle Dokumente für die „weitgehend vergessenen Opfer.“[[17]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-18)

2014/15 nutzte ein Forschungsteam der [Utah State University](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah_State_University "Utah State University") 32 von Dobbertins Fotografien aus den [Usambara-Bergen](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usambara-Berge "Usambara-Berge") als Ausgangspunkt für Diskussionen in der Gemeinde und historische Untersuchungen. Die Forscher führten mündliche Befragungen durch und verglichen frühere und neu aufgenommene Fotografien derselben Orte, um die Veränderungen in der Umwelt und Kultur der Region zu untersuchen.[[19]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-19) In einer anderen Studie desselben Autors wurden Dobbertins Landschaftsfotografien der evangelisch-lutherischen Missionsstation [Mlalo](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mlalo "Mlalo") sowie eines [Trappisten](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zisterzienser_der_strengeren_Observanz "Zisterzienser der strengeren Observanz")klosters und einer Siedlerfarm untersucht. Diese Art der Fotobefragung ergab Aufschlüsse über die kolonialen Veränderungen der natürlichen Umwelt und die lang anhaltenden ökologischen Folgen.[[20]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-20)

Muslim in _Kanzu_ vor einer Moschee-Ruine

In einem Artikel, der 2022 vom Institut für Afrikastudien der Russischen Akademie der Wissenschaften veröffentlicht wurde, analysierte die Historikerin Anastasia A. Banshchikova die Darstellung von Menschen, Militärstationen, Denkmälern und Straßen im europäischen Stil sowohl in anonymen Ansichtskarten als auch in Dobbertins Fotografien von Bagamoyo, der ersten Hauptstadt der deutschen Kolonie. Die Autorin stellte fest, dass afrikanische Muslime und islamische Gebäude wie Moscheen nur selten auf kolonialen Postkarten abgebildet wurden, die eher deutsche koloniale Errungenschaften und Infrastruktur repräsentierten. Im Gegensatz dazu zeigen Dobbertins Fotografien die lokale muslimische Kultur, wie Moscheen[[21]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-21) und Muslime in typischer Kleidung wie _Kanzu_ und _[Kofia](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofia "Kofia")_.[[22]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-22)

In ihrem 2023 erschienenen Buch über die (Wieder-)Aneignung historischer Fotografien im heutigen Tansania berichtet die Historikerin Eliane Kurmann, dass sie Dobbertins Fotografien und Postkarten von Landschaften und Menschen, der kolonialen Infrastruktur und dem Ersten Weltkrieg in ganz Tansania gefunden hatte. Sie werden in Museen ausgestellt, um einen Einblick in die deutsche Kolonialzeit zu geben, und illustrieren Schul- und Geschichtsbücher sowie Websites. Wie Kurmann feststellte, führte Charles Kayoka, ein tansanischer Medienwissenschaftler und Fotograf, ein sogenanntes Re-Picturing-Projekt durch, um die Veränderungen der von Dobbertin fotografierten Orte zu veranschaulichen, indem er dieselben Szenen und Motive 100 Jahre später fotografierte und diese historischen und zeitgenössischen Bilder einander gegenüberstellte.[[5]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:3-5) 2014 wurden diese Arbeiten im deutschen Kulturzentrum [Goethe-Institut](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goethe-Institut "Goethe-Institut") in Daressalaam ausgestellt.[[23]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-23)

In Deutschland befinden sich Fotografien und Postkarten von Dobbertin in den Sammlungen des Bundesarchivs. Im Jahr 2014 wurden fast 1000 Fotografien von Dobbertin durch das Bundesarchiv auf Wikimedia Commons veröffentlicht. Das [Nationalmuseum von Tansania](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalmuseum_von_Tansania "Nationalmuseum von Tansania") besitzt eine Sammlung von 107 Negativen auf fotografischen [Glasplatten](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fotoplatte "Fotoplatte").[[5]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-:3-5) Im Vereinigten Königreich hält die [Cambridge University Library](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_University_Library "Cambridge University Library") eine Sammlung von Postkarten mit Szenen aus Deutsch-Ostafrika von Walther Dobbertin und Carl Vincenti.[[24]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-24) Diese Bibliothek besitzt auch ein Exemplar von Dobbertins Broschüre „Von Deutscher Arbeit in Deutsch-Ostafrika“ aus dem Jahr 1920, die monochrome [Fotogravur](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fotogravur "Fotogravur")-Postkarten mit landwirtschaftlichen und industriellen Motiven aus Deutsch-Ostafrika enthält.[[25]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-25)

In den Vereinigten Staaten existieren Sammlungen von Dobbertins Fotografien in der Bibliothek der [Yale University](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University")[[26]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-26) und in der [Northwestern University](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwestern_University "Northwestern University").[[27]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-27) Neben anderen Fotografien enthält die Sammlung an der Northwestern University ein Album mit Originalabzügen und Postkarten mit dem Titel "Deutschostafrikanische Bilder", die zwischen 1900 und 1910 veröffentlicht wurden. Diese Sammlung dokumentiert die Veränderungen des europäischen Lebens und der Natur in Ostafrika. Die Fotos zeigen insbesondere den Bau von Eisenbahnen, das Wachstum der Städte und die deutsche Kolonialverwaltung. Schließlich wird auf der Webseite auf den kulturellen Kontext der Zeit und des Ortes hingewiesen, an dem die Bilder entstanden sind, und hinzugefügt, dass diese historischen Quellen „auch Materialien enthalten, die anstößige Bilder oder eine Sprache enthalten können, die das Wesen des europäischen Kolonialismus in Afrika widerspiegelt.“[[28]](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walther_Dobbertin#cite_note-28)
